utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Before we resume the examination of witnesses, I'd like to inform you that the Chamber has seen a copy of the letter written by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, addressed to Mr. Ierace. We went through the relevant parts of the transcript. The Chamber is of the opinion that it's beyond our competence what is in this letter. It seems to be a bit of a personalised conflict on something that happened out of this Court. It bears no direct relevance for what has happened in Court. The Chamber expects both parties to continue to communicate with each other. The way it's done is not our major concern. Our major concern is that it is done, and which members of one of the teams will participate in it, or whether you do it by a computer chat session, or whether you do it with a video recorder, recording whatever has been said, is none of our business. This Chamber expects both parties to communicate and to fulfil their duties in respect of the case we're hearing. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to begin with, good morning everybody. I have heard the Chamber's answer and I understood it. And just one thing: The Defence is quite ready, as it has assumed the responsibilities it has undertaken to meet with the Prosecution to discuss matters. I merely wanted the Chamber to know that the Defence is quite ready, of course, if Mr. Ierace is ready to meet us so as to make movement forward. And if we have a personal problem, I am quite sure that we shall be able to resolve it very easily. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber is dealing with two parties: Prosecution and Defence. How they will organise their meetings is not of major concern for this Chamber. What we expect, as a matter of fact, is that, as grown-up professionals - I'm looking to both parties - you'll solve your problems. Thank you. Then I'd say that this issue may be closed for the moment, I hope forever. Mr. Ierace, you may call your next witness, which will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution calls Milada Halili.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll just use the time available at this moment to do some computing. As far as I can see, the witness Ifeta Sahic has been examined during one hour and three minutes, and the cross-examination took one hour and fifteen minutes. As far as the witness Sabri Halili is concerned, the examination-in-chief took one hour and eight minutes and the cross-examination took close to one hour and a half. So I'd like the Defence to keep an eye on the clock. It's more difficult for you to see, but ... yes. Please, Mr. Usher, bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand? I'll put the question again to you. Can you now hear me in a language you can understand? I see no reaction at this moment. Mrs. Halili, can you now hear me in a language you understand? I see some reaction, but can you hear me, Mrs. Halili, in a language you understand? Yes? Would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- answer aloud because nodding cannot be translated and will not be in the transcript of this Court hearing, so if you intend to say "yes," please say "yes" aloud instead of nodding. I see that there is still some problems. Can you hear me, Mr. Usher? THE USHER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you adjust the headphones? Just test again. Yes? It's clear, the noise, the sound? It seems not to be okay yet. Yes? Can you now hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now. It's better now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration at the beginning of your testimony. The text of that declaration will be given to you by the usher. Would you please read it and make the declaration aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mrs. Halili, you will be first examined by Mr. Mundis of the Prosecution team. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, for the record, can you please state your full name and spell your last name, please?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Milada, last name H-a-l-i-l-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, can you please state your date of birth and the city or town in which you were born?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: 12 of December, 1965, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, do you recall approximately when the war broke out in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in what city were you living at that time Ms. Halili?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I was living in -- on Pere Kosarica Square, now the Heroes' Square.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And is that square in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Throughout the course of the war in Bosnia, did you continue to live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, I'd like to draw your attention to June 27th, 1993. Do you remember that day?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you living at that time on the Heroes' Square?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With whom did you live on that date at that location?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I was living there with my mother. However, when the war broke out, since my mother had to cross the bridge and the snipers targeted it, I told her to go to the post office company and sleep there, because I was afraid for her life and I simply did not want to have to think whether she'd get home alive or dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, can you please tell the Trial Chamber your mother's name?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Almasa Konjhodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've made reference to a bridge. Can you tell the Trial Chamber the name of that bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: It's called Malta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, why did you suggest to your mother that she go and sleep at the post office?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Because a sniper from the hill and from Grbavica targeted that bridge and I feared for her life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your mother work at that time? Was she employed at that time, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. She was under labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For whom was your mother employed during 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Public Enterprise Post Telephone and Telegraph Sarajevo, PTT Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your mother actually work in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that is the building that you suggested that she sleep in to avoid the snipers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, are you married currently?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is your husband's name?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Sabri Halili.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On June 27, 1993, did you and your husband, Sabri Halili, take a trip to pick up your mother at the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately what time did you leave your apartment on that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. It was 8.00, perhaps half past. I'm not quite sure when it was that we started, but I know that we went to her place and I took some coffee to her. She was ready, and we immediately set off to go to my mother's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: How far approximately was it from your apartment to the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your husband and yourself then pick up your mother and proceed to her brother's house?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you proceed on foot? That is, were you walking?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far did -- or approximately how long did it take you to walk from the PTT building to your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: About one hour, perhaps an hour and a half, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On that morning, were you able to take a direct route or did you have to take a circuitous route?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No. We had to take a roundabout way because nobody could, nobody dared, nobody did take the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, why did people not take the main street?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Because of the snipers who targeted it from Grbavica. So nobody dared take the main street, and there was no traffic there at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, how did you become aware that snipers were in the Grbavica area?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Because the Chetniks were on Grbavica. They held that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you know that, Ms. Halili?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Well, because there is only a street which separates us, I mean my neighbourhood and Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were snipers the object of much conversation and discussion in Sarajevo in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: There were snipers because my building faces Grbavica shopping, and my flat burnt down from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What exactly is the Grbavica shopping that you indicated?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: It's a skyscraper. It's high-rise buildings, and there was a post office and it was a shopping area. There were a number of shops, and it is where they fired at the Heroes' Square from there, that is, at the flats which faced Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you hear reports of sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Merely for the interpretation. It is not quite clear. Could the witness please be more specific? I do not understand whether she said "my building" or "my apartment." It is merely for the clarity in the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that Mr. Piletta-Zanin can follow the original language of the witness. Would you please clarify that, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated that there were snipers firing from the Grbavica shopping, as you described it, to the building that you were living in. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what was the target that they were shooting at. That is, was it the entire building? Was it your apartment specifically? Can you please tell us what --

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: The building as such, the whole building. They were firing at it. But in October 1992, at that time, my flat burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Halili, were you aware during the course of the war in Bosnia, in Sarajevo in particular, of media reports on the radio or television or in the newspaper about sniping incidents in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, because there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now back to the day that your husband and your mother and yourself were walking to visit your uncle. Do you recall approximately what time you arrived at your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that we left his house around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long you had stayed at your uncle's house on that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I don't know. I never looked at the watch. But what I know is that we had to leave because my mother had to go to work, and it was 12.00 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, do you recall the neighbourhood or the area, what the name of that area was where your uncle lived?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: The street is called Borak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And is that street in a particular neighbourhood of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Between Kovacica and Urjan Dedina, below Tranzit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Halili, when the three of you departed your uncle's apartment - and by "the three of you," I mean yourself, your husband, and your mother - you were returning to the PTT building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the specific route or streets that you took on that morning to return to the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: We went through a school, Valter Peric school. We had to go that way. Then we went behind Skenderija, Dobrovoljacka, then next to the post office on the embankment, then by the central prison behind the Sarajka department store, by the Presidency, and we were moving towards the -- and we headed for the military hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, witness, when you just testified that you went next to the post office on the embankment, is that the post office where your mother Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. worked?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes. No. No. No. That is a different post office. It burnt down in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether on that day you walked past the Marsal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: On our way back, before we reached the intersection where my mother was killed, we could hear a faraway shot, and my mother tripped and she lost her shoe and my husband helped her to get it. And I told my mother - and there was a FAP trailer, because this trailer was not on the ground at all - my mother to start running. However, I was the first one to start to run, and I reached the traffic lights there. When I reached the traffic lights, I only heard my mother call out "Milada." When I turned around, she was already down on her knees. And at that moment when I saw that, I immediately hailed a car. And my husband pulled her to a separate place, and I immediately stopped the car and we put her in the car and took her to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, I'd like to ask you a few specific questions about what happened at that corner. Do you recall seeing -- you mentioned a trailer. Do you recall seeing any other types of barricades at that intersection on that morning or early afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No. Just those containers and that trailer. That's what I saw. And our people had set that up there, because the sniper kept shooting from Grbavica. So they were the barricades and the barriers or covers set up so that people could pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned "those containers" and "that trailer." Do you recall approximately how many containers were located at that intersection on 27 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: There were two containers, and in the middle there was the FAP trailer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you testified a few moments ago about hearing a shot that startled your mother. Do you recall if you heard any other shots after that first gunshot?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No. That second one that was at the intersection, that hit my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified about taking your mother to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened once you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: When I arrived at the hospital, I got straight out of the car and told the nurses to get a stretcher. And when they put my mother on a stretcher, my mother had dentures, and I told them to take her dentures out. I had already seen that she had got a deathly pallor on her and that she was done for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, shortly after the car that you were in arrived at the hospital, that your husband arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After your arrival at the hospital that afternoon, Ms. Halili, did you have any discussions with any doctors or medical personnel about what happened to your mother?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: When I got to the hospital, when we brought her there, the doctor asked me -- Dr. Abdulah Nakas was on duty. He took her in. And he asked me what relationship I was to my mother, and I said I was her mother [as interpreted], but they didn't let me stay in the waiting room close to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if Dr. Nakas or any other medical personnel told you the cause of death of your mother?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: My husband went later on. I went to go and see how my mother was doing. But my husband told me that the doctor said my mother had died and that she had been shot in the main tendon, that she had been hit in her main tendon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness be shown the document marked P1340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis. Yes. Do you have the document in front of you? I have full understanding for the feelings that you will have. It will not be easy for you to be confronted again with what happened in the past to you. So if you feel ready to answer the questions, please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? And if there is any moment that you feel that you need a pause just to recover from the emotions you certainly will have, please let me know immediately. Now, Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, the document which is now before you, which is marked P1340, can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: This is the death certificate for my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you provided a copy of this document by the authorities in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the usher retrieve P1340 from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please take the document from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, do you recall what type of clothing your mother was wearing on the day she was shot?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: She was wearing a red dress with a black tiger on the front of the dress, the print of a black tiger on her dress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how old was your mother at the time she was shot?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Fifty-five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was your mother carrying any kind of weapons or arms on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what you were wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I don't remember. I just remember what my mother was wearing on that day, and I shall always remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, do you recall what your husband was wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your husband was a soldier at that point in time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was your husband wearing any type of military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, because our side didn't have any uniforms, just what they had at home. So they would wear the civilian clothing that they had at home, the civilian uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, when you make reference to "our side," can you please tell the Trial Chamber which side that was, please?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: The Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the morning your husband was shot -- or excuse me, on the morning your mother was shot, was your husband carrying any kind of weapon or military arms?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, because he wasn't on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the intersection where your mother was shot on that morning, do you recall seeing any kind of military equipment or military vehicles in the general vicinity where you were when she was shot?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any soldiers or any individuals in military uniforms at that intersection on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, do you recall meeting with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal in mid-September, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that that investigator provided you with a map of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that investigator asked you to mark the spot where your mother was shot on that map?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the investigator asked you to draw an arrow indicating the direction you were walking at the time your mother was shot?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall if the investigator asked to you mark an arrow on that map indicating where you believe the sniper was at the time he shot your mother?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the usher show the witness the Exhibit marked P3260.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, do you now have the map marked P3260 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature and a date on the lower, right-hand corner of that document?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see the markings that you made on that document with a blue marker?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If the usher could please assist the witness by putting that on the ELMO? And also if she could be provided with a thick, blue marker?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, if you're able to do so, I would like you to put a circle around the markings that you previously made indicating the spot where your mother was shot. Please place a circle around the previous markings.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: It was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you please draw a square box around the previous markings that you made indicating where the sniper was located?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Halili. The usher can return that document to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, I just have a few final questions about your apartment. You testified earlier this morning that your flat had been burned. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what caused your apartment to burn?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: It was in October, when the Chetniks attacked the 11 blue ones and wanted to enter Heroes' Square. That was when my apartment burned down. And from the 15th onwards, quite a number of high-rise buildings, that is to say all five high-rise buildings were on fire at that time. That is to say in October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what caused the fire to start?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: All I know is that I was watching from one of the other skyscrapers, and I watched my apartment burn, and I wasn't able to do anything about it, to save the apartment because there was a lot of shooting. As soon as they saw somebody trying to put out a fire, they would shoot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, you've made reference to five high-rise buildings. Do you recall approximately how --

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- many storeys those buildings had?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Twenty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, do you recall any instances where people were shooting from your apartment building outwards, that is people in your building shooting towards people outside of your building?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No. Because all the people were there -- who were there had families. They were ordinary people afraid for their lives of their families and watched where the shooting was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, referring to the apartment building that you lived in, were there any military headquarters located in that building?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions for Ms. Halili at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, may I just draw your attention to page 11, line 25, on the -- your laptop, and see whether some clarification could be made? You've read that line? Just see whether there is any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, you testified earlier that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas at the hospital. Do you remember when you had a discussion with Dr. Nakas at the hospital on the day your mother was shot?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: My husband talked to him. I just wanted to go in with my mother, but they wouldn't allow me to go in, and he asked me what I was to the woman, and I said I was the daughter, but they said I should stay and wait in the waiting room, and I wasn't allowed to go in the room that they were taking my mother in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Halili. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the French transcript, I don't know whether this is important, but I think at page 17, line 18, the translation does not coincide. I don't know how far the French transcript is of definitive importance. That's my question. So I don't know whether this point ought to be clarified or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no French transcript. What is -- if there is any contradiction, please indicate what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just speaking about the interpretation. I'm not sure that the transcript for the Chamber has any importance in French. Now, if the French transcript is important for the Chamber, then I shall go on with my point. If not, then, I don't mind. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't think that "headquarters," the word "headquarters," was translated properly. In French, the translation was "locaux," which isn't the right translation of the word "headquarters." So I don't know if the French transcript is meritorious or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the French translation is recorded but not written down on paper, but I'm just looking to Madam Registrar, whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My information was not correct. There's a French transcript as well. And please verify whether this remark now made finally will find its way into the transcript, because "locaux" and "headquarters" might not be similar. Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, questions will now be put to you by members of the Defence team, and please be aware that we fully understand how difficult that is for you, and I hope that you have some understanding for the necessity of giving the information which this Court will need to take whatever decisions we have to take. Yes? Are you able to respond to the questions? Yes. Then, Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have a short break, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course you may have. You would just like to leave the courtroom for a second or just have a pause and drink some water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. I'd like to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, we'll just have a break of a couple of minutes. Madam Registrar, what are we usually doing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 9.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Am I right in assuming that the usher is getting the witness? So then we'll wait until she returns. Mrs. Halili, you can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope that this short break helped you to recover from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have full understanding for your feelings, and as we hope you'll have understanding that your information is important for this Court. And therefore we will proceed, but if at any moment you feel you're not able to answer the questions, please let me know. Ms. Pilipovic, you may cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, hello to you.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence would like to convey to you that we feel very sorry for the loss -- for your loss, for the death of your mother. As you said, the war started on the 5th of April 1992, and the war brings nothing but death. How do you know that the war started on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Because shooting started on the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us: When the shooting started in Sarajevo, who started the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: The Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, when you say "the Chetniks," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I mean the Chetniks who were shooting around the city. They were shooting at everything that moved. They were shooting at hospitals. They were shooting at everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Chetniks who were shooting all around the city, could you tell us who these people were?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: These Chetniks, these were the Serbs who were in the mountains, and they were shooting on Sarajevo. The Serbs who stayed in Sarajevo, those were real Serbs, who only had one country, one state, and that was Bosnia-Herzegovina, and those are the real Serbs for me. Those Serbs who shot at us, they are Chetniks. They're not real Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Halili. Mrs. Halili, could you tell us if you remember whether you gave statements to the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I know that the Bosnian police first called me in 1994 or in 1995. I do not remember exactly. But I remember I was called by them, and then I was called nearly every year by the investigators from The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that you gave a statement on the 10th of November, 1995, and if I show you this statement, would you agree with me if I say that you gave that statement then?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that you gave a statement in September 2001, would you agree with me that you gave that statement then?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Considering the time when you gave the first statement in 1995, could you tell us that your memory was perhaps fresher in 1995 rather than in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: In 1995, of course I could remember better.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that your mother worked at the post office?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From what time did she not stay at home?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: From May, she only came to visit, and my husband had to go and get her so they could go over the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you worked in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I was in the BH Army. I was working in the kitchens.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where your place of employment was in relation to your place of residence, if we agree that you lived in 1992 and 1993 in Pere Kosorica Square?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the place where you lived, where was your place of employment?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: My place of employment was in the first skyscraper by a restaurant called Minjon. This is where I distributed meals to the soldiers of the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, in one of those five skyscrapers on the Heroes' Square, there was a location where a BH Army soldiers gathered and that's where you distributed food?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes. They came after they got off guard, and then they ate, and then they went home to rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that you worked in such a place and that you saw soldiers of the BH Army, could you tell me what these soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: They were dressed in civilian clothes because they had no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: They did not bring weapons there because they did not have enough weapons. It was well known that they had one rifle among them, for several soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where did your husband work?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: My husband stood guard but -- around there, but he came home to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the command post of your husband was, where did he go to have his equipment issued, weapons, to receive orders, in relation to his place of residence at the square?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Where the Minjon restaurant was and where these people went, and this is where they changed guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in relation to the square, how many BH soldiers were normally standing guard on that square?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I don't know. All these people who were living there and who had their families there, they were usually standing guard and they were watching over their households.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- in relation to the skyscrapers on the square where the BH Army members were, could you tell me, do you know were there positions of the Republika Srpska army in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: We were only separated by one road from where the Bosnian Army held the positions and the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow us, the Defence would like to have the witness shown a document P3260, and if the witness could mark the position of the BH Army as well as the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you have the black pen available for the witness, since this will be Defence markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Halili, can you see the map?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark for us on this map the location which says "Trg Heroje," Heroes' Square, if that is the street where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And then in relation to that location, if you can mark the positions of the Bosnian Army and then of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, could you tell us, this line above the Grbavica stadium and then this black line which goes along the Topola Osman Pasa [phoen] Street, is that the front line?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes. That was the line, that's where Palma was, and that's where the Bosnian Army was, and then on the Grbavica stadium was -- that's where the Chetniks were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in 1992, 1993, 1994, were there combats in this area?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: In 1992, there was combat when the Chetniks attacked the 11 blue, and they wanted to get the square that was in October. They wanted to cut Sarajevo through.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did they get through to the square?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No. They did not succeed, because the Bosnian Army, our men, defended the place successfully so they would not -- so they would not cut Sarajevo in half.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Considering that you have a map next to you, could you mark for us the bridge that your mother was supposed to take to go to work?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us there, where you underlined Dolac Malta, can you tell us where is the bridge in relation to your apartment and in relation to the post office where your mother worked? Which bridge is that?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: It is between the street of Azize Sacirbegovic, and the Dzajniska [phoen] Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just mark the bridge for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning of the 27th of June, 1993, you said you told us you came to the workplace of your mother where she worked and where she stayed?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark for us where the post office was in relation to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you came to take your mother, you and your husband, you said that you were -- set off in the direction of the street, Urjan Dedina Street?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes. We went then up from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps explain on the map where you had to go, as you said, in order to get to the place where your uncle lived? Which route did you take?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Halili. You have already marked the -- in that portion down there, so by the Ljubljanska Street, so that would be --

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: That it would be between Kovacici and Urjan Dedina. That's below Tranzit Road. That's where my uncle's house was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me whether you took that road before, that you took to get to your uncle's in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: That was the only route that we took to get to my uncle's in the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you think that that was the safest route?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Because all the people went there, cars went there, because they did not dare to go on the main road. Nobody walked along the main route -- along the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the main road was dangerous because of sniping.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, and there was shooting. They could see us on the main road. They could see us as we walked and they could target us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from which side there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: From Grbavica and from the hill, from Hrasno hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether there was shooting from the buildings located in the area opposite Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us on this map where the building of Energoinvest is in relation to Grbavica, if you know, and also if you can show us Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no translation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry. I shall just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was there shooting coming from the direction that you marked as Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, there was no shooting in that direction coming from the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said it was not possible to pass by Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Because the main road is there. We went behind the writers' club. There were containers and there was a main road and they could see us. So that was by the writers' club, and there were containers, so the people could take cover as they were walking by.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew there was shooting coming from the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Because you said you worked in the BH army, you had contact with soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During those contacts with the BH army soldiers, do you know whether the Bosnian army had snipers?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, you said that on 23rd of June there was an incident when your mother was killed. You marked on the map the location where the incident happened. Could you tell us from which direction the bullet came that hit your -- that killed your mother?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: This did not happen on the 23rd. It happened on the 27th of June, 1993. And this bullet came from the white skyscrapers in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see it or hear it?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I heard the shot. My husband told me that the bullet had ricocheted, but I don't think so, because you can see the intersection from the skyscrapers. That's when my mother was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not see the shot coming from the Grbavica skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I could hear it. I had come to the traffic lights when my mother was shot, and when she called out my name she was already on her knees.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said you heard that it came from the Grbavica area and the skyscrapers, could you tell us from which height, in relation to the skyscraper, for which you said they had 20 floors, that the bullet had come from?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that, because I heard the shot and I thought it was very far away. And when my mother called me, I could see that she was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, considering that this is time for a break, is this a good time to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a good time to have a break. Do you have any idea, Ms. Pilipovic, how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will respect the time that it took to have the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a matter of just a couple of minutes? Otherwise we might finish now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes. No. Then we'll have a break now. Then we'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, we will continue your examination by Ms. Pilipovic. You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Pilipovic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, you told us that you had heard the shot when the bullet was fired which hit your mother. Could you describe the intersection where this happened? When I say "describe," can you tell us what buildings are at this intersection?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: There is the Marshal Tito barracks, and across the street is the bus terminal, and that is the route one takes to the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in the Marshal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And the -- were there any people at the bus stop?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: There were, slightly behind it, people who were waiting for the bus to go in the direction of the post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That day, before the critical moment, did you hear any gunfire in that part of the town, as you went through it?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes. A bullet was fired before we reached the intersection. I heard a shot, and it frightened my mother and she tripped, she lost one shoe, and my husband got it. And after that, we heard only one other shot being fired, and that was the one which hit my mother, none other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Today, when asked by my learned friend at 9.32, you said that you saw no military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Anywhere nearby?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember seeing anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness the statement that she gave to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 11th of November, 1995. It is the document 00361312; in B/C/S, it is 00903834. The interpreters have this document, but I also can gave my learned friends the copies of it, both in English and B/C/S. I'd like to show the witness and ask her if she -- if it is her signature on the English version and if it is the document which she signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I assume that this is just to be sure that you're quoting the right document, that you're not tendering into evidence the statement as such, but just in order to verify whether we are all speaking about the same document when you will quote of it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A copy of a document will be now shown to you. Could you please identify whether your signature is under it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please return --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at the second page of the same document? Will you have a look at the page 2 the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then it will be returned to Ms. Pilipovic. Just for technical -- as far as the technicalities are concerned, I don't think that the document has to be marked for identification since they will be quoting literally off it. It was just to be sure that we are all speaking about the same document. Yes, please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness also has the statement in B/C/S. And we can give a copy of this statement to the witness, if she wishes to read what she said. It is page 3, paragraph 2, of the document. The witness can look at it and the Defence can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would rather have you read these lines aloud, just quoting the witness. What now will happen, Mrs. Halili, is that Ms. Pilipovic will read part of the statement you've just seen to you, and may put some questions concerning your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, I will now read to you a part of page 3, that is paragraph 2: "I stopped a civilian car. The soldier who was passing by helped me and my husband to put my mother in the car and take her to the hospital. I was in the car with her, and my husband started to the hospital on foot." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because let me tell you, that guy who was there, he was in civilian clothes, but anyone who was able-bodied, who could take up a rifle and defend it -- so I just naturally thought that he was a soldier. But he was not wearing a uniform. He was wearing civilian clothes. I mean that guy who helped my husband and me to put my mother in the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That person who you said you merely think was a soldier, was that person armed?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is true: Is it true what you said in this statement - and the statement was made in 1995, when you said that your memory was better - that the soldier who was passing by helped you and your husband, or is what you said -- what you answered today to my learned friend true, that you did not remember seeing any soldier? What is true?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I do not remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has explained the inconsistency, to the extent there was one, and we're not necessarily conceding there is. But the witness has explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained. There's no contradiction as such. So the question whether she told the truth at that time or at this time, since there's no contradiction, is not a fair question. So please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your vicinity, when you, your husband, and the soldier who helped you to put your mother in the car, were there any other people around, nearby?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you reported to the official authority, or some official authority, and if so, yes, did you report the incident to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I did not report it to anyone. I merely took her to the hospital. Nothing. I was subsequently called by them. I never reported anything to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: When was it that you were called in the first time, and who was it?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: The Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was that -- if you remember, you told my learned friend that it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: 1994, 1995. I know it is then that I received -- that they called me in. I can't remember exactly, because it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When the doctor said that your mother had died, did you receive any document in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes. I was issued with a document, but I have it at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: In this part of the city, in the skyscrapers where you lived, whatever, all those high-rise buildings, were there any armed operations in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Is there any need for re-examination, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, can you please tell the Trial Chamber what the armed operations that were in your high-rise building in 1992 and 1993 consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, in response to the last question that Ms. Pilipovic asked you, you indicated that there were, in the skyscrapers where you lived, the high-rise buildings, armed operations, in the part -- in this part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you were referring to, please.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I was referring to the 11 Blue who attacked, and when our neighbourhood was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which forces did that attacking?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Chetniks were attacking us because they wanted to take hold of the square. When the 11 Blue attacked, they wanted to take possession of the square because they wanted to cut Sarajevo in two, that is, to take the left bank of the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, with reference to the man who helped you put your mother into the Golf after she was shot, when did you first notice that person?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mrs. Halili, in response to an earlier question asked by Ms. Pilipovic at page 23, line 1, you indicated: "I was in the BH army." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you a soldier or were you a civilian employee?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: I worked in the logistics, that is, worked in the kitchen, and I distributed food to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you wear a military uniform as part of those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. One of my colleagues. Judge Nieto-Navia? I have one more, perhaps two more questions for you, Mrs. Halili.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have several times mentioned the 11 Blue. Could you explain to me what you mean by 11 Blue?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: It is a coffee bar. It is a coffee bar, a tavern, which is called 11 Blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also mentioned that this attack on the 11 Blue took place in October 1992; is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there later on any similar attacks where --

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that means that the actual fighting -- I'm not talking about some shooting now and then, but the actual fighting in October 1992, was that the last time that there was an attempt to take over part of this area of the town by the Serbians?

utterances.speaker: MILADA HALILI
utterances.text: That was the last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mrs. Halili, this concludes your examination as a witness. This Court is fully aware of how difficult it must have been for you, not only to make the very long journey but also to be questioned about events which are very emotional for you. We fully understand that, and we thank you very much for coming, and by giving answers to the questions of the Court and the parties, to provide us with information which is of importance for our considerations and for the decisions we'll have to take. Therefore, I thank you once again very much for coming. I wish you a good journey home, together with your husband. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher will now show you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the admission into evidence is concerned, as far as I can see, we have two documents tendered into evidence, the first one being P1340, which is a death certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And P1340.1, the English translation of the death certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since there is no objection, they are admitted into evidence. Then we have P3260, if I'm correct, Madam Registrar, a map which was marked during both the examination-in-chief and during

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: then. Mr. Mundis, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President. Mr. Ierace will be taking the next witness for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have some observation to make before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. We were talking about exhibits and I believe I heard that the Registrar, every fortnight or so, went through the list of exhibits, and I'm afraid I did not see if the updated list was in our pigeonhole, so I wonder if we could have it, just to avoid any problems?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please inform us about the update?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will provide you with a copy of both exhibit lists tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you from the bottom of my heart. And I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. President, to say that on various occasions Defence requested the assistance of a legal assistant, legal counsel in the court, in order to help us to better systematise our work. However, we have received no reply, and I therefore have to reiterate our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm working on what should be decided on this. I'll try to get -- this Chamber tries to get the proper information and we will come back to it soon. It's not forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Ierace, since there are no other practical matters, Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the next witness? That will be, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Ramiz Velic, Mr. President, and his evidence relates to incident 19 under the sniping schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the answer, I deduce that you even can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration before your testimony. The text will be given to you by the usher now. Would you please make that declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher will give it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr. Velic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ierace of the Prosecution team who has called you as a witness. Mr. Ierace, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please tell the Trial Chamber your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: My name is Ramiz Velic. My father is Arif, my mother is Huma. I was born on the 10th of July, 1943, in Kalinovik, the village of Ljuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In November of 1993, were you living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: I was -- became a car mechanic, but later on, I also learned how to drive, and I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In November of 1993, what did you drive?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: This particular machine is called an ULT 150. It is a loading ladle which loads things on to trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that indeed a piece of heavy equipment, sometimes referred to as a front-end loader?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How long -- I withdraw that. Who employed you to do that, that is to drive the front-end loader?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: My company is called Rad Public Utilities Company, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Since the conflict in Sarajevo commenced in 1992, did you have any duties in relation to the use of that loader and the collection of rubbish?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where did you collect the rubbish from?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on whether there was more rubbish. Where there would be a lot of it, then our superiors would send us to that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Typically, where would the rubbish be? In other words, would it be in a street, in a park, in a rubbish collection centre? What type of terrain?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Well, once again, you know, it varied. It depended on the citizenry or on where people lived, where it was accessible, wherever they would -- there were large containers placed and we would arrive there with big trucks, load it into those trucks and take it away, wherever they would deposit their rubbish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How often during 1993 would you collect rubbish?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Every day. We would be escorted by UNPROFOR if -- or when there was more intensive gunfire or when we went to places which were more dangerous, UNPROFOR would escort us, but we did it every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you were escorted by UNPROFOR, was the escort in the form of individuals on foot or in vehicles or what?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: They would always be two APCs of the UN forces, and at times soldiers would get off the APCs on the ground and sometimes they didn't. On that occasion when I was wounded, I did not see them get off their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before we come to that occasion, by "APCs," do you mean armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the ones that belonged to the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there anything about their appearance which identified them as being part of the UN forces?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, by the colour of the vehicle and the kind of clothing they had, if, that is, they got off the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the colour of the vehicles, that is the APCs?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: White, the colour was white, and it had "UN" marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What were the -- what was the kind of clothing that those forces wore on those occasions when they accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: It depended on the troops, what country they came from, because they had different uniforms. Sometimes camouflage uniforms, helmets, bullet-proof vests, things like that, and sidearms, when and if they got off their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You mentioned a particular occasion. When was that particular occasion, first of all, that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: That was on the 2nd of November, 1993. It was a Tuesday and it was half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On that particular occasion, what part of Sarajevo were you in?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: The street was called Ribarska Street, Ivo Lola Ribar Street, at Grbavica. It is a settlement, and it was called the Trg Heroje, or Heroes' Square.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why had you gone to that area?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: In the morning, when I went to work at 7.00, I received a travel order telling me to go and load up some rubbish in Brace Ribara, and when I arrived there with the full vehicles, the FAP vehicles, the locals from the neighbouring houses helped us load up the rubbish. They used shovels and their hands, and so on. So we cleaned up the rubbish. I filled a truckload of this and started loading up the second truck. And I took up one of the loaders and shovels, went to get another one, and when I was reversing in order to reach the truck, I moved away from one of the buildings. I didn't expect any shooting, but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you please describe the front-end loader, in particular, the part where you operated it from.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to describe. It has four wheels. It has a cabin which is raised up above the ground quite a lot. There is the front loader, in front, the loader or shovel in front, and there is a clutch in the cabin and a button or command that you press to go forward or to reverse. That is located on the left-hand side, and you can only move it -- move that clutch with your left hand. On the right-hand side of the cabin there is another door. There's a door on the right. And you have a lever which enables you to lift the loader, empty it, and generally move it around in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said earlier that there was some shooting. What first made you aware that there was some shooting?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody is conscious and aware of shooting. Anybody who was there could see that there was shooting, and there was shooting every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But you've told us that on this particular occasion you were operating the front-end loader and then there was some shooting. So how did you first become aware, while you were operating the front-end loader, that there was some shooting?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the day that I was wounded, I did not hear the shooting until I was wounded and jumped out of the machine. Because you can hear the noise, actually, from the machine, and the motor. You can hear the motor working. And as I said, while my hand was on the wheel and I was reversing, my hand moved forward. And I didn't actually feel that I had been hit at that particular time. I did this automatically. And I jumped out of the right-hand side of the cabin and took cover. When I was down on the ground, hiding behind the front right tyre, I heard the actual shooting going on, and the sound was similar to when you throw stones on some tin. So that's -- and I saw the bullet holes on the loader, and then I realised that they were actually shooting. And of course, when I saw my hand, I knew what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, as you gave your answer to the last question, you were indicating with your left hand in a circular motion in front of you. Where was your left hand when you first became aware of shooting?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: In front of the steering wheel. The steering wheel was up here, and as I was moving from this angle, my hand was turned towards Vrace. So I suppose that's how it happened, from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: For the benefit of the transcript, the witness indicates the palm of his hand facing downwards, held in front of his chest at about chest height, and then later in his answer to the question indicated to his right, when he said the words "My hand was turned towards Vrace."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You also said earlier that your hand was wounded. Which hand was wounded, your left or your right?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: My left hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've told us that you exited the cabin through the right door and took shelter behind your vehicle. From what direction were you protected when you took shelter on that side of your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: I was protected from the direction in which the bullets were coming from, Vrace. The tyre shielded me, and the loader itself, in fact. I thought that nothing could happen to me if I crouched down and covered -- and used that for cover, although there was shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, in September of last year, that is, 2001, did you return to the area where you were shot in the company of some investigators and film crew and partake in the making of some video film?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ VELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would this be a convenient time to show the video which pertains to this incident? It is Exhibit 3280D, and I think it's the only track on that -- I withdraw that. Yes, that is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please could the technicians start the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: INVESTIGATOR: Please stand where you were sitting in your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. vehicle, to the best of your recollection, when you were shot.
